summary: Describes how to manage early media in SIP using a gateway model and an application server model. It also lists the inputs to consider in setting local policy for generating ringing tones.

plainLanguage.summary: Early media is the sound a caller hears before the callee picks up: a ring tone, a recorded announcement, or the prompt of a voice menu. This memo describes two ways to handle it in SIP, and explains how a phone can avoid losing the first words of the call.

questions: how to manage early media in sip
what is media clipping and how to avoid it

subtitle: How to handle the sound a caller hears before the callee answers, and how not to lose the first words of the call.

tldr.problem: In SIP calls, early media such as a ring tone or a recorded announcement plays before the callee answers. The simple mechanisms in RFC 3261 cause media clipping and problems with call forking.
tldr.mechanism: The memo describes two models: a gateway model that reuses the early dialog created by the INVITE, and an application server model that sets up early media with its own separate offer and answer exchange.
tldr.outcome: The application server model is recommended for most user agents, because it keeps early media apart from regular media and lets the caller mute a ringing tone without risking the start of the call.

today: RFC 3960 is an Informational memo published in December 2004, and the metadata records no obsoleting or updating RFC. It describes two ways to build early media in SIP, and it recommends the application server model for user agents that can tell early media from regular media.

sections.title: What Early Media Is
sections.content:
Early media is audio or video exchanged before the called user accepts the session. Within a SIP dialog it starts when the initial INVITE is sent and ends when the User Agent Server (UAS) produces a final response. It can be one-way or two-way, and it can come from the caller, the callee or both.

Typical early media from the callee is a ringing tone or an announcement such as a queuing status. Early media from the caller is usually voice commands or dual tone multi-frequency (DTMF) tones used to drive an interactive voice response system.

The basic SIP specification, RFC 3261, only supports very simple early media mechanisms, and those have problems with forking and security. This document goes beyond them and describes two models of early media implementation: the gateway model and the application server model.
sections.plainLanguage: Early media is the sound you hear before someone picks up: a ring tone, a recorded announcement, or the prompt of a voice menu. This memo describes two ways to handle it in SIP.

sections.title: Session Establishment and Media Clipping
sections.content:
SIP negotiates session parameters with the offer/answer model. One user agent, the offerer, prepares a session description called the offer; the other, the answerer, replies with a session description called the answer. The two-way handshake lets both user agents agree on the parameters used to exchange media.

Media clipping occurs when the user, or the machine generating media, believes the media session is already established while the establishment is still running. The user starts speaking and the first few syllables, or even the first few words, are lost. Clipping is unavoidable when the offer and answer are exchanged in the 200 (OK) response and the ACK, because the called user starts speaking at the same time as the 200 (OK) is sent, and the UAS cannot send media until the answer arrives in the ACK.

Clipping does not appear in the most common exchange, an INVITE with an offer and a 200 (OK) with an answer. The caller's user agent is ready to play incoming media as soon as it sends the offer, because it cannot count on the 200 (OK) to start playing: signalling and media packets typically traverse different paths, so media packets may arrive before the 200 (OK) response.
sections.plainLanguage: Before any media can flow, the two ends of a SIP call agree on what to send and where to send it. If one end starts talking too early, the first words are lost. That loss is called media clipping, and this memo is largely about avoiding it.

sections.title: The Gateway Model
sections.content:
An offer/answer exchange that takes place before the final response for the INVITE establishes an early media session. That session ends when the final response is sent: if the final response is a 200 (OK), the early media session transitions into a regular media session, and if it is a non-200 class final response, the early media session is simply terminated.

The gateway model manages early media sessions using offer/answer exchanges in reliable provisional responses, PRACKs and UPDATEs. It works well when there is no forking, that is, when the INVITE is not sent to several user agents at once. The caller is ready to play incoming media as soon as it sends the offer, the callee sends the answer in a reliable provisional response, and media can flow straight away.

Forking is where the model breaks down. When the INVITE forks, the caller can receive different answers in provisional responses from different user agents, and early media can arrive from several of them at once. Playing several audio streams together confuses the user, so the caller typically picks one early dialog at random and mutes the rest. If the muted one turns out to be the session that becomes the regular media session, media clipping is likely: the caller has to send an UPDATE with a new offer to unmute it, and the callee cannot send any media until that offer arrives.
sections.plainLanguage: The gateway model reuses the early dialog that the original INVITE created to carry the ringing tone. It works when there is one callee. When a call is forwarded to several phones at once, it breaks down and the caller's words can be lost.

sections.title: When to Generate a Local Ringing Tone
sections.content:
In the traditional telephone network, the local exchange of the callee generates a standardized ringing tone for the caller. SIP user agents have different capabilities, different user interfaces, and may set up sessions with no audio at all, so the way a SIP user agent tells its user about the progress of the call is a matter of local policy. Many user agents imitate a telephone by generating the ringing tone themselves as long as no early media arrives from the callee; if the callee does send early media, the user agent is supposed to play that instead.

The difficulty is that a user agent often cannot tell from the signalling alone whether early media is coming. A simple user agent can send early media without using reliable provisional responses, and a user agent that uses preconditions can send an answer in a reliable provisional response with no intention of sending media. The user agent therefore has to check whether media packets are arriving at a given moment.

The memo suggests a three-step local policy for a telephone-like user agent. Unless a 180 (Ringing) response is received, never generate local ringing. If a 180 (Ringing) has been received but there are no incoming media packets, generate local ringing. If a 180 (Ringing) has been received and there are incoming media packets, play them and do not generate local ringing. A 180 (Ringing) response means the callee is being alerted, and a UAS should send one whenever that is the case, whatever the state of the early media session.

The Alert-Info header field is a separate mechanism. It names an alternative ringing tone for the user agent to use if it decides to generate local ringing, but it does not say when to generate it. The user agent applies the policy above first and only then uses Alert-Info to choose the tone.
sections.plainLanguage: Because SIP gives no clear signal that a ring tone is on its way, the caller's own phone has to decide. The memo gives three rules: stay quiet until a 180 (Ringing) arrives, ring locally if nothing else plays, and stop ringing as soon as audio from the callee arrives.

sections.title: The Application Server Model
sections.content:
In the application server model, the UAS behaves as an application server to establish the early media session with the UAC. The UAC indicates support for the early-session disposition type, specified in RFC 3959, using the early-session option tag. The UAS then knows that it can keep the offer/answer exchange for early media separate from the one for regular media.

Keeping the two exchanges apart helps with forking. The UAC can reject or mute new offers for early media without muting the sessions that will carry media when the original INVITE is accepted, and it can give priority to the media received over those sessions. The transition from early to regular media then happens at the right moment.

A separate exchange also helps the UAC decide about local ringing. If a new early session is established and that early session contains at least one audio stream, the UAC can assume that early media is coming and can avoid generating local ringing. The memo notes that even here a user agent still has to choose which early media sessions to mute and which to render, and it recommends that information which is not essential for the session should not be transmitted using early media. For instance, user agents should not use early media to send special ringing tones, because the SIP status code and reason phrase already inform the remote user about the progress of session establishment.
sections.plainLanguage: The second model gives the ringing tone its own separate setup, distinct from the call itself. That way the caller can turn one off without disturbing the call, and it knows audio is coming before it starts ringing locally.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Both models use the offer/answer model, and that brings the usual SIP security concerns. A user agent sends a session description containing the transport address, an IP address and port, where it wants to receive media, and it then assumes that media arriving at that address comes from the peer it described. An attacker who can gain access to the contents of the SIP message and send packets to that address could interfere, so user agents SHOULD encrypt their session descriptions, for example using S/MIME.

Encryption does not stop an attacker from guessing the transport address, which is sometimes easier than it seems because many user agents always pick the same initial media port. User agents SHOULD therefore use media-level authentication mechanisms such as the Secure Realtime Transport Protocol (SRTP), and those that wish to keep their communications confidential SHOULD use media-level encryption. To stop an attack that makes a user agent send media to a victim, the user agent SHOULD first engage in a handshake with the owner of the transport address, checking only that it is willing to receive media, before sending a large amount of data. That check can use a connection-oriented transport protocol, STUN in an end-to-end fashion, or the key exchange in SRTP.

One risk is specific to early media. When operators let early media through for free but charge for regular media sessions, rogue user agents may try to establish a bidirectional early media session and never send a 200 (OK) response for the INVITE. The memo does not recommend that operators disallow bidirectional early media, because some application servers, such as interactive voice response systems, use it to collect information from callers, for example a calling card PIN code. Instead, operators should consider a remedy of charging early media exchanges that last too long, or stopping them at the media level.
sections.plainLanguage: Early media opens the door to the same attacks as any SIP session: someone who can guess the address a phone listens on can send it fake audio. The memo says to encrypt the signalling, authenticate the media, and check with the far end before sending a lot of data.

items.title: No 180 (Ringing)
items.text: Unless a 180 (Ringing) response is received, never generate local ringing.

items.title: 180 (Ringing) but silence
items.text: If a 180 (Ringing) has been received but there are no incoming media packets, generate local ringing.

items.title: 180 (Ringing) and audio
items.text: If a 180 (Ringing) has been received and there are incoming media packets, play them and do not generate local ringing.
